docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Welcome to Bristol Flight Lab's documentation pages.

This site includes lab admin documentation, and tutorials aimed at our team, postgraduates, and undergraduate students. Find the Flight Lab's main website here.

We're sharing behind-the-scenes docs publicly in case they're of use to anyone - if you find them helpful we'd love to hear about it, and if you spot any errors or would like to suggest changes please do so via an issue or, even better, a pull request.

docs.title: Getting there
docs.text:
No public access

Fenswood Farm is not publicly-accessible, these instructions are for research collaborators and students.

Flying sessions are weather-dependent, so check for confirmation the day before and on the day.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
Fenswood Farm is in the village of Long Ashton, a short journey from central Bristol.

Address: Fenswood Farm, Wild Country Way, Long Ashton BS41 9AG.

Lab entrance: Google Maps / What3Words

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: Options from the University's Clifton campus:

docs.title: Bus (recommended)
docs.text:
The closest bus from the Clifton campus departs from The Centre, approximately 10 minutes’ walk from Queen’s Building. These buses start at Bristol Bus Station, and head through the centre of town via Anchor Road. The journey from Anchor Road takes around 15 minutes, followed by an additional 5-minute walk down Wild Country Lane to Fenswood Farm.

Route (timetable linked):

  • X9 towards Nailsea

The service runs approximately every 30 minutes, and timetables can be checked via the Travelwest or First Bus apps for the most accurate, real-time information. You may pay by contactless on the bus, but tickets are cheaper in advance via the First Bus app.

If you're not familiar with UK buses: raise your arm clearly to hail the bus to stop, otherwise it will go past you! The bus will head out of Bristol and into Long Ashton village, and after you've passed the village centre you'll see a '30' speed limit sign, then a zebra crossing - ding the bell for the bus to stop when you see ahead that the houses stop and trees and fields start. Get off the bus at Warren Lane, just as the bus leaves Long Ashton village.

docs.title: Bicycle
docs.text: Cycling is also a good option, and National Cycle Route 33 takes you from the city centre right past Fenswood Farm.

docs.title: Taxi
docs.text: Taxis average around £15–£20 each way from the Clifton campus. Local taxis are bookable via the Veezu app; Uber and other apps also operate in Bristol.

docs.title: Driving
docs.text: Limited parking is available at the farm, so please plan accordingly and car-share where possible.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
Access is UCard controlled, and staff only - students and visitors should contact staff on arrival.

The Lab entrance (and parking) is on the south side of the building - turn right through the main gate, along the side of the main building and round to the left.

docs.title: Open CV
docs.text:
OpenCV (Open Source Computer Vision Library) is an open-source computer vision and machine learning software library. It provides a wide range of tools for image processing, video analysis, and computer vision applications such as face detection, object tracking, and motion analysis.

This page will focus on using in a python environment, but the same functionality is available in other languages such as C++ as well.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Image Processing: Filtering, transformations, edge detection, and color space conversions.
  • Object Detection: Pre-trained models for face, eyes, and pedestrian detection.
  • Video Analysis: Motion tracking, background subtraction, and optical flow.
  • Machine Learning: Integration with models for classification and clustering.
  • Cross-Platform: Works on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS.
  • Language Support: Bindings are available for C++, Python, Java, and MATLAB.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Using pip, the module can be installed with 'pip install opencv-python'. For more install info see here: https://opencv.org/get-started/

To check you're install is correct run a basic example

import cv2 as cv
img = cv.imread("path/to/image")
cv.imshow("Display window", img)
k = cv.waitKey(0)

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
To help learn there are some exercises located in this github repo: https://github.com/incognitopikachu/opencv-workshop

You can use git to clone it locally, or just download it as a zip if you're unfamiliar with git (option under green 'Code' button)

All the exercises are in the 'exercises.py' file.

To follow along you'll need to use the opencv docs: https://docs.opencv.org/4.x/ Note that the documentation normally lists functions with their C++ syntax, but there will always be an equivilent python function. The library is well used so google, stackoverflow and LLMs will help you find the answer.

docs.title: Photogramatory
docs.text:
To make accurate measuremnets, understanding how a 3D point, X in the real world gets projected onto a 2D point, x in the image is essential.

This relationship is described by two key matrices:

1 Intrinsic Matrix (Camera Matrix) K 2 Extrinsic Matrix (Pose: Rotation + Translation), [R|t]

x = K [R|t] X

docs.title: Intrinsic Matrix
docs.text:
The intrinsic matrix encodes the internal parameters of the camera — the characteristics that describe how it forms an image from incoming light. It tells us how 3D points in camera coordinates are projected onto the 2D image plane (pixels).

K = \ \begin{array}{} fx & 0 & cx\\ 0 & fy & cy\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} Symbol Meaning fx, fy Focal lengths (in pixels) along x and y axes. cx, cy Coordinates of the optical center (principal point).

Note, that the focal lengths here refer to the pixel scaled focal length.

docs.title: Camera Calibration with Open CV
docs.text:
These parameters can be calculated during a calibration process which uses a checkerboard pattern.

Note that changing zoom and autofocus setings can change the intirnsic matrix.

docs.title: Extrinsic Matrix
docs.text:
The extrinsic matrix describes the camera’s position and orientation relative to the world (or object) coordinate system. It converts coordinates from world space → camera space.

R|t = \ \begin{matrix}{} r_{11} & r_{12} & r_{13} & t_x\\ r_{21} & r_{22} & r_{23} & t_y\\ r_{31} & r_{32} & r_{33} & t_z \end{matrix} Symbol Meaning ( R ) 3×3 rotation matrix (orientation of the camera). ( t ) 3×1 translation vector (position of the camera).

On a drone, these parameters can be calculated using GPS, IMU and altimeters readings. More more precise measurements, a technique called Structure from Motion may be used to calcualte parameters from existing images.

docs.title: Pi 5 Setup Workshop
docs.text:
• Hostname: pi5-group1
  • Username: pi
  • Pwd: flightlab

docs.title: 1. Flash the SD card
docs.text:
1. Install Raspberry Pi Imager on your laptop
  2. Choose Raspberry Pi 5, then Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit), then your SD card.
  3. On the customisation screen, set:
  4. hostname, username and password (from the table above)
  5. Wi-Fi SSID, password and country
  6. locale and timezone
  7. Enable SSH (password authentication is fine for now)
  8. Write the card. You will probably need to reformat the sd card at this step. This will take a few minutes.

While it writes, connect the camera to the Pi. The Pi 5 uses the smaller 22-pin camera connector. Check the ribbon orientation against the guide before you power up, because a ribbon in the wrong way round is the most common reason the camera isn't found. Camera documentation.

docs.title: 2. First boot
docs.text:
Plug in the screen, keyboard and SD card, then power on. The first boot takes a couple of minutes and may restart once.

Open a terminal:

hostname                 # should match your table
hostname -I              # your IP address, so write it down
ping -c 3 google.com     # check you're online
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y

docs.title: 3. SSH from your laptop (Only if using autonomous network - won't work on eduroam)
docs.text:
Windows, macOS and Linux all have ssh built in. Open a terminal (PowerShell on Windows):

ssh <username>@<hostname>.local

If that can't find the Pi, use the IP address instead: ssh <username>@<ip>. Type yes the first time it asks about the fingerprint.

docs.title: Optional SSH Step - Set up a key so you don't have to type your password every time
docs.text:
On your laptop:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519            # press Enter to accept the defaults
ssh-copy-id <username>@<hostname>.local

Windows doesn't have ssh-copy-id, so use this in PowerShell:

type $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub | ssh <username>@<hostname>.local "mkdir -p ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"

Log out and back in. You shouldn't be asked for a password.

Recommended: install the VS Code Remote-SSH extension so you can edit files on the Pi directly: https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/remote/ssh

Checkpoint: before moving on, you should be able to log in over SSH without typing a password.

docs.title: 4. Camera from the command line
docs.text:
Plug the camera in with the ribbon cable. Do this when the pi is not powered on.

Try these on the Pi's own screen first:

rpicam-hello --list-cameras       # is the camera detected?
rpicam-hello -t 0                 # live preview, Ctrl+C to stop
rpicam-still -o test.jpg          # take a photo
rpicam-vid -t 5000 -o test.h264   # 5 seconds of video

If using SSH there's no screen to show a preview on, so add -n:

rpicam-still -n -o test.jpg

Then copy the image to your laptop to view it. Run this on the laptop:

scp <username>@<hostname>.local:~/test.jpg .

The images are probably blurry, this is a good point to play with the focus settings (physical not software) as you will need to adjust this in future.

docs.title: 5. Python: Picamera2 and OpenCV
docs.text:
sudo apt install -y python3-opencv
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages ~/cv-env
source ~/cv-env/bin/activate

Don't skip --system-site-packages. Picamera2 is installed system-wide, so a plain venv won't find it.

Save this as capture.py and run it with python capture.py:

from picamera2 import Picamera2
import cv2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_preview_configuration(main={"format": "RGB888", "size": (640, 480)})
picam2.configure(config)
picam2.start()

frame = picam2.capture_array()
print(frame.shape)
cv2.imwrite("frame.jpg", frame)

picam2.stop()

Note: Picamera2's RGB888 format is stored in BGR order, which is what OpenCV expects. So if your colours look swapped somewhere, this is probably why.

Stretch goal: convert the frame to HSV, threshold it on a cube colour, and draw a bounding box around the largest blob. Save the result to a file.

docs.title: 6. Shut down properly
docs.text:
sudo poweroff

Wait for the green LED to stop flashing before you pull the power. Pulling the plug while it's running is the easiest way to corrupt the SD card.

docs.title: If something's not working
docs.text: Problem Try No cameras available Power off, reseat the ribbon, check orientation and that it's the 22-pin cable Could not resolve hostname Use the IP address instead of .local Connection refused SSH isn't enabled: sudo raspi-config → Interface Options → SSH REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED You re-flashed the card. Run ssh-keygen -R <hostname>.local on your laptop No module named picamera2 Your venv is missing --system-site-packages. Delete it and recreate it Lightning bolt icon on screen The power supply isn't good enough, so use the official 27W one
